blocks.note: The spine of the project. This header is the whole map in nine lines, and it is worth reading before the code: START, then preparar, then the orchestrator, then the specialists from the plan one at a time, then the writer, then the check, and from there either the spreadsheet and the end, or back to the writer, and after two refusals the emergency answer. Line 12 draws the line that matters most: the orchestrator, the specialists and the writer use AI. Everything else is plain code.

randomUUID is used on line 107, writeFile only at the very bottom for the drawing. Then LangChain and LangGraph. The five message classes are the vocabulary of the conversation: HumanMessage is you, AIMessage is the model, SystemMessage is the instructions, ToolMessage is a tool's answer, and RemoveMessage is a marker that deletes a message from the saved history, used on line 245. SqliteSaver writes the state to a file, and ChatOpenAI is the OpenAI client shape, pointed at Ollama on line 68.

Your own files. AGENTES and the planning helpers come from harness/agentes.ts, which holds every prompt. listarPreferencias from harness/dados.ts reads the stored preferences. The four names from harness/ferramentas.ts are the tool side: the Caderno type, the one-line flight description, the argument cleaner and the servicos object. anotar and rastrear are the Langfuse hooks. The four from harness/verificador.ts are the answer checks.

Reads .env relative to this file rather than to the folder you ran the command from, which is why "node harness/agente.ts" works from anywhere. bot.ts does the same thing with a plain ".env" and is therefore pickier about where you start it.

The four limits, each with its reason in the comment. Six steps per specialist caps one agent inside one request. Fourteen steps per request caps all of them together, so four specialists cannot quietly cost you twenty-four model calls. Two retries is how many refused answers the writer may fix. Six hours is how long a searched price stays usable. These four numbers are the difference between a bot and a runaway bill.

LangGraph needs to know, for every field of the state, how to merge the old value with whatever a step returns. This helper says "the new value simply replaces the old one" and sets a starting value. Writing it once keeps the state below readable instead of repeating a reducer on every line.

The state: the folder that travels through every step. Line 48 brings in the one field with different merge behaviour, since messages are appended rather than replaced. Then: voos is everything searched and still valid, which the analysis tools read; novos is what has not reached a spreadsheet yet; pesquisadoEm is when the last search happened, compared against the six-hour limit; buscas are the searches already made, which is what blocks a repeat; plano is who still has to work, first in the list being the current one; idioma is the answer's language; recados are the notes the specialists leave for the writer; passos and passosDoAgente are the two counters; tentativas is how many answers the checker refused; and correcao is the note for the next model call, kept deliberately outside the conversation so a failed attempt does not pollute the saved history.

The model, and the trick the comment names: Ollama Cloud speaks the same protocol as OpenAI, so the OpenAI client works once baseURL points at ollama.com/v1 and the key comes from OLLAMA_API_KEY. The model name comes from MODELO in .env, defaulting to glm-5.3, and that one variable is what lets harness/avaliar.ts grade several models against the same exam. The two-minute timeout bounds a single call.

The conversation is stored forever, but sending all of it would cost money on every call, so only the last forty messages go out. The subtlety is where to cut: a tool answer without the request that asked for it is rejected by the model, so the cut has to land on one of your own messages. findIndex looks for the first human message inside that window, and line 78 falls back to the last human message for the rare case of one round longer than the whole limit. Exported because teste.ts checks exactly this.

From older rounds this keeps only the questions and the real answers, dropping all the tool traffic. inicioDoPedido is where the current round starts, and everything from there on is kept whole. Before that point it keeps your messages, and model messages only when they carry no tool_calls, which is how it tells a finished answer from a tool request. Less noise for a weaker model to lose itself in.

Just the text of your own messages inside the window. It is handed to the tools so they can check a date or a city was really said, and to the checker so a price you typed can be told apart from a price a tool returned.

The conversation id lives in config.configurable.thread_id, which LangGraph threads through every step, and in Slack that is the channel. preferenciasDe uses it to read that conversation's stored preferences and keep only the texts.

Three lines fixing a real bug, and the comment explains it: Ollama returns ids like "chatcmpl-283" that repeat across calls, and to LangGraph a repeated id means "replace that message". Without a fresh id, a new answer would silently delete an older message from the conversation. Every model answer added to the state goes through this first, and teste.ts checks that two calls produce two different ids.

The first step of every request. velhos is true when the last search is older than six hours. Everything is reset: the plan, the language, the notes, all four counters, the correction note and the search list. The last two lines are the interesting ones: the flights are either kept or thrown away based on velhos, which is what stops yesterday's price turning up in today's answer.

One model call that decides who works, and nothing from it enters the conversation, so a bad plan leaves no trace. temVoos tells the model whether anything is searched already. bindTools with tool_choice "required" forces it to answer by calling definir_plano instead of writing prose. Line 136 reads the arguments, and if the call is missing it falls back to planoDoTexto, which scrapes agent names out of the text. planoValido then throws away invented and duplicated names and puts the rest in a fixed order. Both live in harness/agentes.ts.

A factory, not a step: it takes an agent name and returns the step function for that agent, which is why four specialists are one piece of code. Line 145 pulls that agent's tools and instructions out of AGENTES in harness/agentes.ts, and those are the only tools this specialist will ever see.

The exit. It drops itself from the plan with slice(1), resets its own step counter and the correction, and appends what it wrote to recados, unless the note is just "pronto". That is the other half of the NAO_RESPONDA instruction in harness/agentes.ts, which tells every specialist to finish with "pronto" or one sentence about what was missing. The useful sentence reaches the writer; the empty acknowledgement is dropped.

The guard. If this specialist has already used its six steps, or the request has used its fourteen, it leaves immediately with "ran out of steps" as its note, which the writer then turns into an honest answer. Without this line, a model that keeps asking for tools would loop until the bill noticed.

Building the letter to the model: this agent's instructions, plus any stored preferences appended to them, plus the cleaned history. The correction note goes in last as a human message, which is how a specialist is told "you did not call the tool properly, try again" without that scolding ever entering the saved conversation.

The model call, with only this agent's tools bound. If it asked for tools, the step returns the message plus the counters, and the conditional edge on line 315 routes it to the tools step. This is the normal, happy path.

What a weaker model actually does when it fails, in three flavours: invalid_tool_calls, which is a malformed call; a call typed out as text, caught by escreveuChamada in harness/verificador.ts; or a promise to search without searching, caught by prometeuSemFazer in the same file. Rather than accepting any of that, it sets a correction note and lets the same agent try again, which costs one step out of six.
The normal exit: whatever the model wrote becomes this specialist's note, and the agent leaves the plan.

The step that actually runs the tools, one call at a time and in order. The comment gives the reason it is not parallel: several simultaneous Google searches invite a block. It is exported because teste.ts drives it directly, which is how the cross-agent tool block gets tested without a model.

The last message holds the tool calls. Then the scratchpad the tools read and write: the current flights, the new ones, a copy of the search list, your own texts plus the stored preferences, and the conversation id. Line 183 copies buscas with the spread for the reason in the comment: a step must not mutate the state object it was handed, so the tools write to the copy and line 210 hands that copy back as the new value.
The enforcement point of the whole team design. permitidas is the tool list of whichever agent is first in the plan, and nothing else is reachable from this step, no matter what the model asked for.

For each requested call: look the name up in the allowed list, and line 194 throws a readable error naming the tools that are allowed when it is not there. Line 196 then runs it, with limparArgumentos stripping the nulls and empty strings weak models send for optional fields, and the scratchpad riding in through config so every tool can reach it. Zod validates the arguments at this point, and a bad argument throws here.

The catch is one of the most important four lines in the project: an error does not crash the request, it becomes the tool's result text, prefixed with "Erro: ". That is what lets the model read "the date is not in the request" and ask you instead of guessing, and it is why every error message in harness/ferramentas.ts is written as an instruction rather than a complaint. The result is then logged and wrapped in a ToolMessage carrying the id of the call it answers.

Handing everything back to the state: the tool answers, the updated flights, the updated search list, and pesquisadoEm set to now only if a real search happened, which line 205 detects by comparing the lengths. If nothing was searched, the old timestamp stays, so the six-hour clock is not reset by an analysis-only request.

The writer, and the only step whose output you ever read. It has no tools at all, which is the whole point: it can only use what the others brought back. instrucoesDoRedator in harness/agentes.ts gets the language, the preferences and the specialists' notes. The correction note is appended when the checker refused the previous attempt, and line 221 clears it so the next step does not see it twice.

The last barrier before Slack. The last message is the candidate answer, everything before it is the evidence, and line 229 cleans the text for Slack with arrumarParaSlack so the checks see exactly the text that would be posted.

Assembling the facts. doPedido deliberately starts at your last message, so a price from an older round cannot be used to launder a new claim. retornos is every tool answer inside that window. Line 233 is the one hand-written exception in the system: the cost-benefit rule lives in the writer's instructions, so the writer is allowed to quote it, and it is pasted into the facts to make that legal. Line 234 joins the tool answers, every known flight described one per line, and that rule into a single blob the checker searches.

doUsuario is what you wrote, kept separate so your own numbers can be treated differently. links is every address from anything that is not your own message, plus every flight link, and the comment says why: a link you typed must not be repeated back as if the bot found it, which is what stops a phishing link being laundered through the bot. Line 239 runs the real check in harness/verificador.ts, and line 240 is approval: the cleaned text is written back under the same id, replacing the message in place.

The refusal path. It logs the problems, scores them in Langfuse as "verificador_recusou" so harness/aprender.ts can rank them later, and then does the thing that makes retries safe: RemoveMessage deletes the bad answer from the saved history, so a refused answer never becomes context for the next attempt. tentativas goes up, and the correction note hands the writer its own refused text plus the list of problems plus an instruction to write the whole answer again.

The emergency answer, reached when the writer failed every attempt. It is written by code, not by the model: with flights, it says it could not write the answer safely and pastes the raw search summary from resumirVoos; with nothing, it asks you to rephrase. Uglier than a model answer, and the numbers are real, which is the right trade. It also scores itself in Langfuse, so you can see how often it happens.

The spreadsheet step. The comment is the reasoning: code creates it, so it is never forgotten, never created twice, and the link is never invented. Line 265 returns an empty object when there is nothing new, which changes nothing in the state. Line 267 builds the route list for the title, deduplicated through a Set.

The call goes through servicos (harness/ferramentas.ts) rather than directly to planilha.ts, which is what lets the exam fake it. On success, the link is appended to the answer under the same message id, so you get one message rather than two, and novos is cleared. On failure, the error is appended instead and novos is deliberately left alone, so the next message tries again. That is how a Google outage costs you a sentence rather than the whole search.

The first routing function: go to whoever is first in the plan, or to the writer when the plan is empty. It is used in two places, after the orchestrator and after the tools, which is what makes a specialist loop between its model call and its tools until it leaves the plan.

After a specialist: if it asked for tools, go run them; otherwise follow the plan, which may be the same agent again if it has not exited yet. That single line is the "model and tools, back and forth" loop described in the header.

After the check: no correction means approved, so go create the spreadsheet. Otherwise back to the writer while tentativas is still within the limit, and to the emergency answer once it is not. This is the only place the retry count is read.

The checkpointer, and the comment names what it buys: the whole state is written to a file after every single step, which is the memory that survives Ctrl+C. The path comes from MEMORIA in .env or memoria.sqlite next to this folder, and setting MEMORIA=:memory: is how teste.ts and harness/avaliar.ts stay away from your real conversations. Lines 297 and 298 list the possible destinations, which LangGraph requires declared for conditional edges.

Registering the steps. Eleven nodes, and notice lines 303 to 306: the four specialists are four calls to the same factory with different names, so adding a fifth agent means one line here and one entry in harness/agentes.ts.

The arrows, which match the header comment line for line. Plain edges where the path is fixed, conditional edges where a function decides. The four specialist lines all use the same decider, the tools step rejoins the plan, the writer always goes to the check, and the check branches three ways. Line 324 compiles it with the checkpointer, which validates the shape and hands back something runnable. Nothing has executed yet at this point.

What you see in Slack while the graph works. The progress callback type, then a function that turns a tool call into a human line: a search names the route and date, a multi-day search names the range, a new watch names the route, and anything else becomes "Analisando os voos...". This is the only place in the project where emoji codes are written by hand.

Running the graph. callbacks comes from harness/rastreio.ts and is an empty array when Langfuse is off, so there is no branching here. stream runs the same graph as invoke but yields each step as it finishes, which is what makes live progress possible at all. recursionLimit 60 is LangGraph's own emergency brake, set well above your own limits so it only fires if one of yours fails. The two loops look for tool calls in each step's output and report them. Then the final state is read back and the text of its last message is returned.

The function bot.ts calls, and the conversation id becomes thread_id, which is what gives every channel its own memory. Lines 357 to 359 handle the case most bots get wrong: if the saved state still has a next step, the bot died mid-request, so that request is finished first and its answer is put in front of the new one, because it may carry a spreadsheet link you never saw. Then your new message runs. Line 362 falls back to a readable sentence if the result is somehow empty.

Terminal use, two modes. With an argument it answers one question under the conversation id "terminal", printing progress as it goes, which is the cheapest way to test a change without Slack. With no argument it asks LangGraph to describe itself and writes harness/agente.html, the same Mermaid trick as grafo.ts. Because the picture is generated from the real graph, it cannot drift out of date: change an edge above and the drawing changes with it.
